item.title: From Life-History Model to Theories of Ecological Diversity: The Impact of Madhav Gadgil's Work
item.description:
arXiv:2611.16042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we review and provide perspectives on the foundational contributions of the renowned ecologist Madhav Gadgil, including the Gadgil--Bossert life
obreakdash-history model, ecological diversity, population biology, harvesting theory, human--ecological systems, co
obreakdash-evolution, adaptive management, and environmental democracy. We outline the key theoretical developments arising from these works and discuss their continued influence on contemporary ecological thought and present
obreakdash-day ecological systems.
item.dc:creator: Arni S. R. Rao, Harman Jaggi, Shripad Tuljapurkar

item.title: Counting doubly labelled trees and one-component networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.16186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A phylogenetic network is one-component if the child of every reticulation is a leaf. This class of networks has been widely used as building blocks in the combinatorial study of phylogenetic networks. We establish a bijection between one-component networks on $k$ taxa and rooted binary multi-labelled trees in which every label occurs exactly twice. Using this bijection and Burnside's lemma, we derive a closed formula and a two-term recurrence for the number of one-component networks. We further obtain explicit formulas for counting one-component networks with a prescribed number of reticulations.
item.dc:creator: Louxin Zhang

item.title: Diversification under Global Competition: A Cutoff-Induced Localization Mechanism
item.description: arXiv:2611.16887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Niche differentiation promotes biological diversity but does not necessarily eliminate competition for shared limiting resources. What determines the extent of diversity when evolutionary diversification takes place under such constraints? We investigate this question using a simple, analytically tractable model combining mutations in continuous trait space, local competition, and global competition for shared resources. We show that, without an establishment threshold, the population spreads indefinitely in trait space even as its total abundance approaches a finite limit. In contrast, an arbitrarily small establishment threshold allows a stable localized distribution. Together with mortality induced by global competition, the threshold creates bistability, and global feedback drives the system exponentially close to the Maxwell point, where an isolated invasion front is stationary. The resulting soliton has height $H\propto\varepsilon^{2/3}$ and width $W\propto\varepsilon^{-2/3}$. Simulations with discrete individuals reveal an archipelago of fluctuating clusters whose spatial extent eventually reaches statistical saturation, unlike the continuous deterministic soliton. Nevertheless, an effective cutoff $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eff}}\simeq0.8/(N\sqrt{\mu})$ reproduces the observed scaling of the population mass deficit. Remarkably, both occupied trait-site richness and effective species richness exhibit approximately the same scaling as the deterministic soliton width. Thus, deterministic cutoff theory captures global diversity scaling despite failing to reproduce the community's spatial organization.
item.dc:creator: David A. Kessler, Nadav M. Shnerb

item.title: Stability of equilibria in discrete-time modified-gradient systems and the multivariate breeder's equation
item.description:
arXiv:2611.14756v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The multivariate breeder's equation $\Delta ar z=G
abla\ln ar W$ is a widely used discrete-time modified-gradient system describing the evolution of continuous traits in organisms. This system could more conventionally be expressed as $x_{k+1}=x_k+P_k
abla f(x_k)$. For its continuous-time counterpart $x'=P(t)
abla f(x)$, it has been proven that an isolated local maximum of $f$ is uniformly stable whenever $P(t)$ is positive semidefinite, as is the case for the "$G$-matrix." Furthermore, the continuous time system is uniformly asymptotically stable when the maximum is an isolated critical point and $\int_0^\infty\lambda_1(P(t))\,dt=\infty$. We show that the literal discrete analog of this result is false: with constant positive definite $P$ the iterates can oscillate or diverge. The result is restored by a single additional hypothesis, a uniform bound on the largest eigenvalue of $P_k$, $\lambda_n$, such that $\lambda_n(P_k)\le 2/L$ where $L$ is a local Lipschitz constant of $
abla f$. Under this bound the maximum is uniformly stable; under a stricter version together with $\sum_k\lambda_1(P_k)=\infty$, the maximum is uniformly asymptotically stable. Given these hypotheses, a level-set estimate of the basin of attraction carries over. Both bounds are sharp, and each remaining hypothesis is shown to be necessary. Biologically, the bound says that genetic variance in every direction must be small relative to the curvature of log mean fitness; outside this regime the mean phenotype can overshoot a fitness peak as hypothesized by Fisher's geometric model. As further application of our results, the same conditions apply to the mean update of Gaussian evolutionary optimization algorithms, in which the covariance of the search population plays the role of $G$.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin J. Ridenhour

item.title: Universal Infectious Disease Forecasting with Mantis 2
item.description: arXiv:2611.16935v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Public health agencies need to anticipate how outbreaks will unfold, when they will peak, and how long demand on health services will remain elevated. We previously developed a foundation model, Mantis, which was trained entirely on simulated outbreaks---enabling us to generate the diversity and scale of training data needed to support forecasting across diseases. However, our previous work left unresolved when simulation improves predictions and how it should complement observational data. Here, we varied the balance of simulated and observed training data while holding forecasting tasks fixed and varying the available surveillance history. We found that simulation-rich training was particularly valuable with limited local history, and its relative advantage diminished as more observations became available. We also found that simulation-based training reduced exceptionally large forecast errors, suggesting that mechanistic knowledge can help compensate for limited local evidence. Building on these findings, we developed Mantis 2, which combines simulated and observational training to jointly forecast up to six variables sixteen weeks ahead. Across 30 forecasting tasks, Mantis 2 achieved the best aggregate probabilistic accuracy over short, medium, and long horizons among the machine learning, statistical, and baseline models evaluated. It missed roughly 30\% fewer outbreak peaks than the strongest comparison model, with successfully anticipated peaks identified more than six weeks in advance on average. We publicly release Mantis 2, enabling public health agencies and researchers to forecast disease outcomes without developing a separate model for each disease or location.
item.dc:creator: Carson Dudley, Reiden Magdaleno, Yutong Bi, Anthony Valencia, Xiaofeng Liu, Marisa Eisenberg

item.title: Species differences dilute the stabilizing effect of higher-order interactions in competitive communities
item.description: arXiv:2501.09172v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Higher-order interactions, in which the presence of a third species modulates the interaction between two others, have been proposed as a mechanism that stabilizes ecological communities. In particular, in models of intransitive competition, replacing pairwise contests by three-way contests turns neutral oscillations into a stable coexistence equilibrium. Whether this stabilizing effect survives in more realistic scenarios, when pairwise and higher-order interactions act together, species differ in their demographic rates, and interactions take place on a network remains unclear. Here, we study a competitive community model with a tunable fraction $\alpha$ of higher-order interactions, combining Lyapunov and linear stability analysis with numerical simulations and empirical birth and mortality rates of plants. For identical species, any $\alpha>0$ makes the coexistence equilibrium globally stable. Differences among species in the ratio of birth to mortality rates, instead, make pairwise competition actively destabilizing and shift the transition to a finite critical fraction $\alpha_c$, which grows with the variance of these ratios. For larger differences, a feasible equilibrium often ceases to exist and, when it exists, higher-order interactions frequently fail to stabilize it. Even when stable, the coexistence equilibrium is often only one of two attractors near the transition, so that robust coexistence requires a larger fraction of higher-order interactions. On sparse random hypergraphs, a finite fraction is needed even for identical species: coexistence requires each individual to take part, on average, in more than one higher-order interaction, well beyond the percolation of hyperlinks. Our results show that the claimed stabilizing effect of higher-order interactions is fragile, and depends jointly on species differences and on the structure of interactions.
item.dc:creator: Marc Duran-Sala, Sandro Meloni, Violeta Calleja-Solanas

item.title: Evolution of cooperation in multiplex interaction networks
item.description: arXiv:2606.00196v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Across biological and social systems, preferential interactions among similar individuals can promote cooperation. To account for real-world interactions unfolding across multiple, simultaneous dimensions, we develop a framework for the evolution of cooperation in multiplex networks. Each layer is defined by a distinct phenotypic trait, with homophily favoring encounters between similar partners. We derive analytical conditions for natural selection to favor cooperation when phenotypes are independent or exhibit epistasis, allowing for different modes of mutation coupling. Despite payoffs being aggregated across layers, the cooperation conditions separate by layer under weak selection. Each condition depends on local payoffs and a structure coefficient determined by the effective number of phenotypes and the mutation rates. Epistasis restricts the phenotypes available on a layer and can thus shift its strategy distribution relative to that of its isolated counterpart. We show that phenotypic diversity fosters cooperation by partitioning populations into assortative niches. Furthermore, in finite populations, intensifying the prisoner's dilemma shifts the dependence of cooperation on strategy mutation from a monotonic decrease, through a U-shaped response, to a monotonic increase. Beyond weak selection, simulations show that accumulated payoffs across layers can alter mean cooperation relative to isolated systems even when phenotypes are independent. Our study unravels how homophily based on multiple phenotypes can shape the evolution of cooperation in heterogeneous populations.
item.dc:creator: Zijie Chen, Xingru Chen, Feng Fu

item.title: ADZE 2.0: rarefaction estimates of allelic richness and private allelic richness for whole-genome data
item.description: arXiv:2611.12472v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Allelic richness and private allelic richness describe how alleles are distributed across populations, but both depend strongly on sample size. Rarefaction makes them comparable by computing the expected number of alleles in subsamples of a common size, and ADZE implemented this approach and an extension to alleles shared only by a set of populations. However, ADZE was developed for microsatellite data and cannot read sequencing data in variant call format (VCF). Here we present ADZE 2.0, which reads VCF, computes each statistic genome-wide or in genomic windows, and can treat blocks of phased SNPs as haplotype alleles. We also implement improved memory handling and multi-threading support. ADZE 2.0 reproduces the ADZE 1.0 estimates for human microsatellite data exactly. On chromosome 22 of the high-coverage 1000 Genomes Project data, private allelic richness for all 325 population pairs took 4.4 minutes on 32 threads. ADZE 2.0 is available at https://github.com/szpiech/ADZE.
item.dc:creator: Zachary A. Szpiech

item.title: Collaboration drives phase transitions towards cooperation in prisoner's dilemma
item.description: arXiv:2602.11601v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The emergence of cooperation among self-interested individuals is a central puzzle across biology and the social sciences. While evolutionary game theory has identified mechanisms such as spatial structure and group selection to sustain cooperation in the prisoner's dilemma, most models assume individuals revise their strategies independently. In reality, social organisms frequently form temporary coalitions to coordinate their decisions. We introduce a \emph{collaboration ring model} to investigate how such joint strategy updating affects the prisoner's dilemma. Individuals update strategies either alone---choosing a best response---or by forming coalitions where actions change only if every member is at least as well off and at least one is strictly better off. Despite individual incentives favouring defection, we show that cooperation emerges through non-equilibrium phase transitions governed by the propensity to collaborate and the benefit of cooperation. Below a critical threshold, defection dominates; above it, cooperation persists through a continuous or a discontinuous transition. Using pair approximation, we derive phase boundaries that align closely with stochastic simulations. Finally, we demonstrate that these results are robust to variations in neighbourhood and coalition size, suggesting that collaborative decision-making is a general mechanism for sustaining cooperation. Our work has potential connections to both the mutualism phenomenon in non-humans and the shared intentionality phenomenon in humans.
item.dc:creator: Joy Das Bairagya, Jonathan Newton, Sagar Chakraborty

item.title: A five-species counterexample to the Hofbauer--Kon--Saito conjecture on qualitative permanence
item.description: arXiv:2610.38374v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hofbauer, Kon and Saito showed that a Lotka-Volterra interaction matrix $A$ with negative diagonal can be qualitatively permanent only if (C1) every cycle of length $\ge 2$ of $A$ is nonpositive and (C2) every negative cycle contains exactly one negative entry. They conjectured that these conditions are also sufficient, and proved this for $n\le 3$. We give a $5\times 5$ integer matrix with seven nonzero off-diagonal entries that satisfies (C1) and (C2) but is not qualitatively permanent. For an explicit integer growth vector, in which one species is an obligate consumer as the definition allows, the system has an interior equilibrium, and an asymptotically stable heteroclinic cycle on the boundary of the orthant attracts an open set of interior orbits. Adding non-interacting species gives counterexamples for every $n\ge 5$. The interactions form a one-way feedback loop together with a predator of two prey. The verification is elementary except for one heteroclinic connection, which lies in a face that is not Volterra-Lyapunov stable. For it we prove a connection lemma based on invasion graphs, which reduces the question to a smaller, stable face. The failure is robust. It persists under small perturbations, including weak additional interactions, so every sign pattern that satisfies (C1) and (C2) and contains ours is a counterexample, and it occurs for an open cone of growth vectors. For $n\ge 6$ there are also counterexamples in which every species grows when alone. Finally, we announce that the conjecture holds for $n=4$ and that, for $n=5$, four minimal sign patterns characterise its failure.
item.dc:creator: Miruna-Mihaela Beldiman, Andrei-Dan Halanay

item.title: Nonequilibrium Transient Centers in Continuous-Time Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.41930v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Analysis of mathematical models in ecology and epidemiology often emphasizes asymptotic dynamics, such as stable equilibria, periodic orbits, and attractors. However, many biologically relevant trajectories exhibit long transient dynamics in which a relevant observable evolves slowly for an extended period before a comparatively rapid transition occurs. On finite time scales relevant to data collection, management, and intervention, such transient behavior can be more informative than the eventual asymptotic outcome. In this work, we study long-lasting and slowly varying transient dynamics in continuous-time systems through the framework of nonequilibrium transient centers. These centers are points in the state space near which the observable can remain nearly constant for a long time, even when the full state is not near an equilibrium. We develop finite-time escape criteria for identifying such centers and their reachable counterparts. These criteria provide practical conditions under which nearby trajectories can remain in a slow regime for a long period of time before eventually leaving it. We apply the theory to an epidemic model with delay of stability loss. In this model, trajectories may remain close to the disease-free manifold for a long time before the infectious population resurges. The framework developed here describes this behavior as slow evolution near a nonequilibrium transient center followed by finite-time escape from the slow regime.
item.dc:creator: Anthony Pasion, Felicia Magpantay
